questions.question: Define globalisation and explain its causes using the lesson's two-family structure, with one worked mechanism per family.
questions.expected_answer: Globalisation is the growing interconnection and interdependence of the world's economies — goods, services, money, people and information flowing across borders so national economies function as parts of one world economy (test: decisions on one continent quickly change prices and jobs on another). Technology family made it possible: e.g. containerisation — a standard box moving ship-to-truck-to-train without unpacking collapsed transport costs, making distant manufacturing profitable; cables and the internet made information instant, enabling global value chains. Policy family made it permitted: tariffs negotiated down (producing the WTO in 1995), finance freed from exchange controls, and closed economies — China, the Soviet bloc, post-1994 South Africa — rejoining world markets.

questions.question: Present globalisation's two-sided scorecard for South Africa — two gains and two losses with evidence — and state the balanced verdict.
questions.expected_answer: Gains: world-scale motor industry built by global carmakers supporting over 100 000 jobs; lower consumer prices and wider choice from open trade (an unannounced raise on every wage); plus faster technology spread and foreign capital funding our savings shortfall. Losses: clothing and textile towns like Newcastle lost tens of thousands of jobs to cheap imports after tariffs fell; contagion — the 2008 foreign financial crisis cost South African jobs within a year; uneven distribution of gains and pressure on the tax base from mobile multinationals. Verdict: globalisation grows the total while redistributing the shares, so policy must capture gains while protecting and re-skilling the losers — never a simple for-or-against.

questions.question: Explain the North/South divide through its three mechanisms, and give two developments that are changing the divide.
questions.expected_answer: The divide is the persistent economic gap between the developed North and developing South (economic shorthand, not strict geography). Mechanisms: terms of trade — the South sells raw and buys made, and raw exports tend to buy fewer manufactured imports over time (the coffee example: beans for cents, roasting and branding for rands); debt — Southern borrowing in foreign currency balloons when world rates rise or currencies fall, squeezing social spending; voice — IMF, World Bank and WTO rules were historically written with Northern voting power, e.g. tariffs higher on processed than raw goods, discouraging Southern industrialisation. Changing it: the rise of China/India shifting the economic centre southward, BRICS pressing for Southern voice, and the AfCFTA building Africa's internal market so the finishing stays in Africa.
